notes.title: Playtest build April 2025 now live!
notes.content:
Hello captains! We have a new playtest build with some big updates on the hook for ya.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44951977/a8963fd9799d6af845404299460a6767eb5c2381.png

New features

 Save games! Not the most exciting feature but something that has taken a lot of effort to get in. You can now open the pause menu when not in the tutorial or combat to save the game. The game is also saved when entering and leaving a harbour.
 A new Rift has been spotted out at sea! This one is still in development but we would like your feedback on what we have made so far. We are quite excited to hear what you think.
 New starting ship: The glass cannon Tarpon
 Rumours now have their own page in the journal
 Streamlined creating your captain
 More things to take with you in the life boat when starting a new run
 You can now name your ship when starting a new run
 More narrative content
 More sound effects
 More crew traits
 More Auxiliary Equipment with a wider range of effects
 Traits and Auxiliary Equipment now impact challenge difficulty
 Crew responding to one of their crew mates dying or being marooned


Bug fixes

 Captain no longer leaves because of low mood. Thanks for reporting it @Rasmus and @copakindred!


Known issues

 Crew for hire gets shuffled if exiting the Inn, even though you have bought them drinks
 Occasionally monsters fly in the tutorial
 Log entries do not not get saved


Unknown issues?

 Probably a lot of fun bugs with save games we haven’t found yet. Do jump on our Discord and tell us if you find any :D 


Looking forward to hear what you think!

- Skipper Alex

New features

Fixes

notes.title: Thanks for your feedback! Here's what's next
notes.content:
Ahoy captains it's been great seeing you enjoying the latest playtest and come with suggestions for what can be improved. I've looked over all the feedback including the Let's Play videos (damn we suddendly got some traction!) and have come up with this list which is what we will focus on in the next month or so:

Tutorial & gameplay verbs not taught well

 Zooming. Fix: Show hint in tutorial, rightside permanent hint, start camera a bit zoomed out
 Turning sails. Fix: Move that part of the tutorial to be after lode anchor when sailing to port, rightside permanent hint
 Difficult to understand sails are not fully deployed. Fix: Make the input a bit snappier, tutoriali\e it better
 Bits of the journal can be accessed too soon. Fix: Disable them until reaching the first port
 Difficult to understand how to install equipment. Fix: Hint directly in the hover text

Keyboard+mouse input wonky

 Cannot use ESC as back action Fix: have it work as back button until the only logical step is to open the Pause menu
 One player would like to invert zoom when scrolling
 Be able to right click to unassign stamina points

Quests & Map

 If marker is outside edge of map difficult to know where to go. Fix: Dotted line to marker
 If having multiple quests it is not obvious what quest is active. Fix: Have quest headline underneath map marker

Ease of use

 Using the back action as a third UI option to for example install equipment is not intuitive. Fix: Assign new keybindings to it for controller and keyboard
 Be able to invert zoom input in Options
 Need better feedback crew has to get paid. Fix: Add a hint label to the harbour overview UI that the player needs to pay the crew before they can leave.
 No feedback when a rumour has been followed up on: Fix: Small XP reward when chasing up rumour and list it in the captain's log
 Crew member status widgets does not highlight text
 Morning duties assignment gets tedious to do again and again. Fix: Make animation faster, select the lock in button to start with

Balancing

 Economy is a too generous. Fix: Make quests pay less

Combat

 Need to make combat more varied. Fix: I got a bunch of ideas how to fix this that all tie into each other so will share more at a later point

Not being able to tilt camera up above horizon line

 Will be time consuming to solve in terms of technical issues with draw distance and rendering the horizon but worth testing out how it would make the game feel if the camera was more free and then decide if we want to make the change

We are planning on releasing another build this week with some of these fixes in and enable access to the playtest again. 

Safe winds
- Captain Alex

notes.title: Dev Log 5 - Preparing for our first showcase
notes.content:
Hello, we are back with another dev log. This time, with an update on what we have been up to over the last couple of weeks and some news about our first public showcase!

Ship and monster models 2.0
Sofie, our artist, has been busy getting updated models for ships and monsters into the game, as we are aiming for a more gritty visual tone than what we initially had. The pirate faction in the game is also using captured ships from other factions, so we have been working on how to portray that. Yes, this is an Imperial ship but it is being crewed by seagoing scoundrels, so we show this by painting them in more rusty and grimy colors.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/c11054968582fa3ef6153c4abbd3de952dd482ad.png

The ship hulls have also been updated to have more pronounced silhouettes to make them look less cute at a distance.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/a756f59837040553a71300ebae0f362d10e38f23.png

The Needler enemy also got a redesign to look more fierce and hostile. Sofie has drawn inspiration from deep-sea anglerfish in her redesign. It’s quite scary-looking, if I should say so myself!

Preparing for our first showcase
We have been selected to showcase Sea Of Rifts at Copenhagen Gaming Week in the upcoming weekend, which is quite exciting since it’s the first time we will show the game to the public. Some work has gone into polishing the game, with our writer Fergus getting familiar with the in-house tools Alex has created to make narrative content for the game.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/a0b0523b14156e94907dc505192a92ec8a274a23.png
A writer stoically facing his worst fear, the empty page

On top of that, we also wanted to have something that would draw people into our booth and therefore decided to make a custom rudder controller for the game! The next blog post will be about how it was showcasing the game and will go into more detail on how we built the controller and got it connected to the game.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/de5717789c5971a15a087769ccb94462beba4e76.png

That’s all for this time. Please give us a wishlist if you haven’t already :)

notes.title: Dev Log 4 - Our internal tools
notes.content:
Hello again, mateys! Alex is back with another tale of brave game development. Today, I'm going to talk about the in-house tools I've made that allow us to create Sea Of Rifts.

I love making tools. It's very satisfying to have a workflow that works just right and is perfectly suited for your own needs. Here is what we needed the tools to do:

 Make it easier to test the game 
 A lot of the game is generated only when the game is played making it difficult to debug. Therefore providing ways to visualise the generation is very useful.
 Allow non programmers to create content for the game
 Not take too long to develop They can be a bit rough as long as they are functional

Debug menu

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/24d24f519e6fae65881d63fa0451b24e0376c0ca.png
The simplest but most used tool we have is the in-game debug menu. This allows us to easily, for example, injure a crewmember or give the player a specific item to test interactions in the game. If you're starting out on your own game, I highly recommend you put a debug menu into your game early. I've made mine so it's easy to add new options by calling a single method:

At some point, I also want to add that the content of the buttons can be dynamically changed so there can be toggle and multi-state buttons.

It’s also worth noting we can start the game in a debug mode where the ship is already populated with crew, and they can also be automatically assigned to duties so you can get right into testing the game.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/0bea7f96d2cea11f636c774dda46bf231f95aecb.png

ProcGen Visualization

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/4e23f7ae1e6e563b0bde74b850be7bbb2e467076.gif

Often the first step to understand a programming problem is to visualise it. I therefore wanted an easy way to show an image with custom information inside the game. Luckily for me, we already had a place to do that - the in-game map! With some switch statements inside the map UI code, it's easy to add more data to view and then use the debug menu to choose between them. We use this to visualise places for world events to spawn, how wakes are rendered after ships, where to place trees, and so on.

Narrative tools

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/9768e9108ba6a786520e23dec281f6375f35c35e.png
Sea of Rifts is all about creating memorable stories for the player. We have a bunch of different mechanics in the game to create these, and they all need content created for them. Thankfully, we are making the game in the Unity engine, and it is fairly easy to write your own editor windows for it. This is a lot better than, for example, having the data come from text files or spreadsheets, since you are sure the data is valid, and it can also be a much more rewarding workflow for the person working with it. The first one I made was to hook gameplay up to Ink, the narrative scripting language we use in the game:

This allows us to write out the interaction in Ink and then hook it up with the gameplay. Choices made by the player can change parameters in the game state, and skill tests done by the crew result in different outcomes triggered. For writing Ink we are using the default Inky editor.

If you want to know more about how tools can help you in your own game, then I did a talk some years ago on the topic that’s still worth a watch. 

That’s all for this time! Please give Sea Of Rifts a wishlist if you haven’t already :)

notes.title: Dev Log 3 - NPC ships, ahoy!
notes.content:
Hello, landlubbers! It’s Alex back with another dev update. This time, it’s about our newest gameplay feature: NPC ships!

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/dc10b2c9bd3087300ff981021da26ea0895606be.gif
What zombies and sea monsters have in common
Have you ever thought about why zombies are so popular in video games? I think one reason is that they are easy to code. If you see a zombie do something that puts them in danger, it doesn’t go against the way we imagine a zombie to behave, since they are primarily driven by their lust for tasty brains. For the same reason, when I was prototyping Sea Of Rifts, I also started out with making monsters chase the player instead of other ships. It was simply easier and quicker to make than ships, since we expect a vessel crewed by other humans to behave more intelligently than a monster just following instinct.

This meant the combat could be prototyped quicker, but I also found out that they don’t make for interesting antagonists in the more narrative sense, since they can’t have as much character as other ships. With other ships, the player can build a relationship with the other captain and to the factions that they belong to. Since we are working towards having the game generate deeper stories, we therefore needed NPC ships.

I started out with defining the requirements for the system to drive the behavior of the ships:

- Use a common data structure so both the player and NPCs use the same data for their ships and weapons.
- Not too complicated to write.
- Something that can be extended with more behaviors as need be.
- Ships from different factions can interact with each other without involvement from the player.
- Didn’t need to be super performant since I don’t think we will have a lot of ships on screen at the same time

Therefore I split the system up into three groups: decision making, locomotion, and combat:

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/9ae9ceb77643e7f0e204e93f1576f1c0d79c9b52.png
For the decision making, I ended up with a mixture of boid steering used for simulating flocking behaviors and utility AI. If you are interested, AI In Games has a great video on utility AI by the way. It also took some refactoring of the existing code used to steer the player ship to make it modular and plug into the steering code. The end system consists of a ship controller component that finds the behavior that has the highest utility and then uses the movement components to apply that movement.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/2a8b1e77b56d4133c7dcd14041bc7e1513e79273.png
As you can see at the start of this post, it has worked out quite well! It’s going to be fun when we have more ships and factions in the game to tune the behavior so each ship gets to have more personality.

That’s it for this time! Please give us a wishlist if you haven’t already :)

Hello hello mateys! It is Alex again this time with a little update on what we have been busy with the last couple of weeks.

SHIP SILHOUETTE DESIGN 
 {STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/84c011edbe19548e5fab867dd3b714831fa24066.png

 [center]

A new feature that was also added recently is the map is now slowly revealed. A fog of discoverability if you will to half borrow a term from strategy games.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/1d1eec552a668a1b95240542e6b449b244d41a31.png

This week I also did a playtest. It's been about a month since the last time we tested so it was about time to get feedback on the game again. The tester is a fellow game designer, so there were a lot of good ideas on how to make the tutorial better, and improve the readability of the game.

notes.title: Dev Log 1 - Starting on the journey
notes.content:
Hello landlubbers welcome to our dev log! it is Alex, the captain on the good ship that is Sea Of Rifts. In this first post I thought it would be fun to write about what the inspiration for the game was and how I figured out what should be at the core of the experience.

A CAPTAIN, THEIR SHIP, AND THE CREW
Back in 2021 I was reading the Tales of the Ketty Jay, a fun and pulpy fantasy series about a captain and his motley crew of misfits, that through shared struggles become a family and learn to trust each other. Being a fan of Rimworld, the idea struck me of taking the social simulation popular in story generators, and put it on a ship. Another reference was the Space Western Firefly. Here we also have a captain and his crew taking on odd jobs and trying to make ends meet. Firefly really excels at making the crew feel like a found family under the guidance of the captain, and the ship being a shared home. Therefore having some crew management ala FTL also entered the mix. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/75cfad05e46d241ce115900629cb087009cdac23.pngThe gameplay inspirations for the game

Yes there was also some inspiration from Failbetter’s excellent Sunless Sea but I wanted to lean more into simulation and procedural techniques to create a dynamic world for the player to explore and discover stories in. Being a fan of tabletop role playing games probably also carried an influence there. I thought using the player’s imagination to bring the world to life was very enticing, so I also decided that a lot of the game would be conveyed through text and abstract systems.

THE FIRST PROTOTYPE
But what should this game really be about? What should the pillars be? Even though I decided to prototype the idea for fun, I also wanted to make sure I created something that would stand out among other games out there. One of the first things I made, was therefore this diagram to compare existing games with each other and see if the concept would stand out.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/4463d876516fa9267ac1d2385dfda36995de242d.pngComparing the concept with existing games

From this it became clear the social simulation of the crew and exploring the world were the most important features. Afterwards I also made this yarn ball of a diagram to get an idea of all the systems and features in the game, and how they would relate to each other. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/aab0d33ca55117898dce55cb90ac69988a649565.pngThis was just a sketch of what I thought the game would be at the time so take it with a grain of (sea)salt.

Normally when making games you focus on the core loop, that is the actions the player do all the time, first and keep Iterating until that feels right to play and then you add more systems on top of that. However since the game was going to be so systems driven, I decided to go a different tack and go broad instead. I needed to see how systems would interplay with each other, before I could get a better picture of how the whole game would play. I therefore often only did a single iteration on a system and moved on to the next part of the game even though I knew it wasn’t working exactly as intended.  

I’m glad I did it this way because it has turned out that some systems could be quite shallow, but I could only figure that out once they had been put in and started to interact with the rest of the game. After a couple of months I had a ship that could move around, the basic world generation working and a ship inhabited by crew members.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44778071/c700fc9f5969bd6649f6da9b941a0ce2e382ceb6.pngThere was crew before there were harbours. No time ashore for these poor sods!

In coming blog posts I’ll explain more about how various aspects of the game works. I think the procedural world generation and storytelling systems for instance are pretty cool, so they will defo get their own posts later on.

If you have made it this far please help us out with wishlisting the game. It helps with visibility on Steam so we can reach more players :)
